newsitem.title: DENMARK: Nordic governments hit back at clashing bikers.
newsitem.headline: Nordic governments hit back at clashing bikers.

text.p: Nordic governments, fed up with rival motorcycle gangs turning one of Europe's most peaceful regions into a battlefield, are fighting back.

They have begun squeezing the bikers, who often resort to the use of rockets, bombs and guns, out of their cities and are considering a total ban on such gangs. They also want to adopt tougher police powers.

Denmark, shaken by an inter-gang anti-tank missile attack in the heart of Copenhagen on Sunday, expects an emergency bill to ban gang clubhouses from residential areas to become law by next weekend and is considering outlawing the gangs altogether, a justice ministry official told Reuters on Monday.

The bill, rushed to parliament last Friday, was a response to bomb, grenade and machine gun raids on biker clubs sited near family homes and it is likely to be followed by new police powers to tap phones and raid properties without a warrant.
"This isn't Denmark, this is war," Copenhagen police chief Hanne Bech Hansen told reporters after the shoulder-fired missile tore into a Hell's Angels' party at the gang's main city base on Sunday.
A man and woman died in the attack and one of the 19 wounded was still in a critical condition, police said.

The raid was the bloodiest yet in months of escalating violence between the dominant Hell's Angels and the rival Bandidos. The clashes have left Danes and their Nordic neighbours wondering what became of peaceful, tolerant society.
"I simply don't understand it. It is not the Denmark I know," Danish Justice Minister Bjoern Westh said on Sunday.
In Sweden police moved swiftly after a bomb exploded next to a Hell's Angels stronghold in the port of Malmo last Thursday, injuring three adults and a baby in nearby homes.

Gang members were ordered out of that property and another clubhouse, about 60 km (40 miles) away in the village of Hasslarp, which was hit the previous Saturday by its fourth rocket attack in 15 months. Police said that the bikers left both properties quietly on Sunday night.
A batch of 12 Carl Gustav, shoulder-fired, anti-tank missiles of the type used in the Copenhagen attack was stolen from a Swedish army store near Malmo in February, 1994.
Missiles identified as from the stolen batch were fired at two Hell's Angels' clubhouses in Denmark last April.
Swedish Justice Minister Laila Freivalds said last week his country would consider banning biker clubs from populated areas.

Norway, which has also seen its share of biker bloodshed, beefed up surveillance of local biker headquarters after the Copenhagen missile attack and will also examine the Danish legislation to see if it could be adopted.

"We shall ask Denmark for more information on the specific provisions of its bill. Then we will judge if it is something we might want," deputy state attorney Tor-Aksel Busch told the Norwegian news agency NTB.
Conflict between the gangs, both local offshoots of U.S. groups with extensive European networks, began almost as soon as the Bandidos set up shop in the region in the summer of 1993.

In February 1994 a member of the Hell's Angels-affiliated Rednecks died in a gunfight after walking -- reportedly by accident -- into a Bandidos meeting at a night club in the Swedish port of Helsingborg.

The then newly elected president of the Bandidos, Mikael Ljunggren, was killed by a sniper as he road his motorcycle north of the city in July 1995 in an ambush that investigators said could have been either a Hells Angels attack or the work of fellow gang members opposed to his leadership.
In March this year, attackers shot a Bandidos leader in the Finnish capital, Helsinki, and a Danish Bandido died in an ambush outside Copenhagen airport 10 days later.
A Danish Bandidos member was shot in the head near the Norwegian city of Drammen in July.
